Annihilation vs. exhaustion: speed and target, not attack and defense

A reading-heavy session (read ~25 min, lesson ~15 min). One win: classify any campaign on the two axes, and stop reading "aggressive" as "annihilation".

Why this lesson

Your First Punic War analysis called both sides' way "annihilation", because both were "aggressively seizing land". That's the most natural mistake there is: annihilation sounds like the aggressive strategy. This lesson takes the two axes apart again, so that "who is attacking?" and "which strategy?" become separate questions.

Block 1: read first

Reading

Echevarria, Military Strategy: A Very Short Introduction:

  1. Chapter 2, "Annihilation and dislocation": the opening and the section "Annihilation" (Cannae, then Ulm). Dislocation and "the indirect approach" are optional.
  2. Chapter 3, "Attrition and exhaustion": the opening, the section "Attrition" (first three paragraphs are enough), and the section "Exhaustion" in full (blockades, Fabius, Washington).

Hold these questions while you read; answer them in the boxes below.

Cannae was a complete annihilation battle. Why didn't it win Hannibal the war? Use Echevarria's term for his mistake.

Rome didn't negotiate: the Senate voted not to, and kept raising legions. Hannibal assumed Rome would act the way defeated states traditionally did: the "Hannibalic fallacy", a wrong assumption about the opponent. Bonus: Cannae still improved his position (allies defected), and the war moved into a protracted phase.

Echevarria says exhaustion "suits the basic nature of defense". Why, in his words or yours? Does that mean only defenders use it?

Clausewitz: the defender "need merely to survive" and make the attacker weary, while the attacker must subdue the defender. Not only defenders: blockades and sieges are forms of exhaustion an attacker uses (the chapter lists them). Credit for "suits" ≠ "only".

What surprised or confused you in the reading?

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

The two axes, again (from the reading)

Start from the definitions, which have no conditions attached [1]:

  • Annihilation aims to win quickly "by severely reducing or eliminating an opponent's material strength through one or two major battles" (Ch. 2).
  • Attrition means "destroying an opponent's forces faster than they can be replaced, while at the same time ensuring one's own rate of loss remains bearable" (Ch. 3).
  • Exhaustion is "wearing down a foe's willingness to fight", "a form of psychological attrition" (Ch. 3).

Read the definitions again and look for the words attack, offensive, defend. They aren't there. Every definition answers only two questions: what is being destroyed (material strength, or willingness to fight) and how fast (one or two battles, or a grind over time). Who is attacking isn't one of the axes.

So what can you conclude about an army that is on the offensive, advancing and taking territory?

Attacking tells you neither what is targeted nor how fast. The Allies in the Second World War were advancing on the Axis capitals, and Echevarria calls their strategy attrition [1, Ch. 3]. Rome besieging Carthaginian cities in Sicily was attacking, and sieges are a form of exhaustion [1, Ch. 3]. Napoleon's offensive at Ulm was annihilation [1, Ch. 2].

The reverse is true too: a defender can fight an annihilation battle. In 255 BCE, Carthage was the defender in Africa when Xanthippus, a Spartan mercenary, used elephants and cavalry to destroy the Roman invasion army: Polybius says only about 2,000 Romans escaped [2, 1.32–34]. One big battle that eliminated the enemy force: annihilation, by the side defending its home.

Levels: a battle inside a campaign inside a war

Your instinct wasn't wrong. It was aimed at the wrong level. Echevarria nests the types [1, Ch. 1]:

"we might design a battle of encirclement and annihilation as part of a campaign of dislocation, which, in turn, might contribute to an overall strategy of attrition or exhaustion."

So each claim has to say which level it's about. Cannae is an annihilation battle; the Second Punic War around it became a long struggle for allies, a slow war [1, Ch. 2]. A quick strategy that doesn't break the enemy's will turns into a slow one.

Your war, phase by phase (Polybius, Book I [2]). Which type is each, by its main mechanism?

Regulus's invasion was a bet on a quick knockout (and it failed); Xanthippus's battle was an annihilation by the defender; a siege is a form of exhaustion [1, Ch. 3]; and the war as a whole was won by grinding down Carthage's capacity to fight, in the end its ability to supply its forces by sea [2, 1.62]. You can argue the whole-war line as exhaustion, since Carthage chose to make peace, but your analysis feedback showed its will held while its capacity broke.

Find the step where this argument goes wrong.

  1. Rome fought aggressively for 24 years, invading Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia.
  2. An aggressive war of conquest is a strategy of annihilation.
  3. So Rome's way in the First Punic War was annihilation.
  4. So Rome expected to win in one or two battles.

Step 2 confuses attacking with a type. Annihilation is defined by speed (one or two battles) and target (material strength), not by who attacks [1, Ch. 2]. Step 4 is the giveaway: Rome clearly didn't expect that; the war lasted 24 years.

Retrieve it

Without looking back: name the two axes every strategy type sits on, and give one example where the attacker used a slow strategy and one where the defender used a quick one.

Axes: target (capacity/material strength vs. will) and speed (one or two battles vs. over time). Slow attacker: the Allies in WWII (attrition), any siege or blockade (exhaustion), Rome at Lilybaeum. Quick defender: Xanthippus 255 BCE; others fine if correct. Got it = both axes named, no attack/defense axis, one correct example of each.
